rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention window will guide subsequent narrowing, slope adjustments, and temperature scouting.
The first method already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while measuring the critical pair’s response to slope.
Both runs achieved the maximum CRF, but the shorter gradient leaves little resolution margin. Raise temperature one step to test whether retention can be shortened without losing full resolution.
The temperature increase shortened retention and improved the critical middle pair. Test another 5 °C increase while monitoring the shrinking separation of the first two peaks.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce initial retention while slightly flattening the gradient. This may shorten elution while preserving the middle pair’s resolution; the first pair will also be monitored closely.
Increasing the starting organic fraction shortened elution and improved every adjacent resolution. Continue one grid step higher to seek a faster method retaining the maximum CRF.

Advance the starting organic fraction another grid step to shorten the run while maintaining a relatively shallow gradient. Check whether the early pair retains adequate separation as it approaches the column dead time.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction to shorten elution while retaining the maximum score. Both the early pair and the middle pair are approaching their resolution limits, so this probes the useful upper boundary for phi0.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a substantially faster gradient for a shorter fully resolved alternative. Lowering phi0 one step protects early retention, while the steep gradient probes whether the critical middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal.

The 2-minute gradient compressed two pairs below baseline resolution. Test a 6-minute gradient between that failed condition and the fully resolved 8-minute method to locate the faster resolution boundary.

Test a distinct fast-gradient selectivity regime: lower temperature may separate the critical middle pair on the opposite side of its order reversal, while lower starting organic should improve early-pair retention. The maximum CRF remains secured by several previous methods.

Lower phi1 to make the 6-minute gradient shallower and recover the critical middle pair’s resolution. The endpoint remains well above the observed elution window, so all six compounds should elute during the gradient.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a different selectivity regime for a faster fully resolved method. A higher starting organic fraction and lower temperature may separate the middle pair after an order reversal, while the 4-minute gradient should improve late-pair separation relative to injection 11.

Test whether higher starting organic separates the critical middle pair on the reversed-order branch while shortening elution. The early pair has substantial resolution margin at 25 °C, but its compression near the dead time will determine whether this approach is viable.

Keep the promising low-temperature selectivity but narrow the gradient window to improve the middle pair’s resolution without further compressing the early peaks. The new endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.60 in injection 14.

Trim injection 8’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope exactly. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient.

At phi0 0.40, flattening the gradient barely improved the critical pair, so test temperature-driven selectivity instead. Compare with injection 14 to see whether a faster, fully resolved alternative exists, while monitoring compression of the early peaks.

Return to the fully resolved 50 °C regime and test a compact gradient with more resolution margin than injection 16. Lowering phi0 protects the early pair, while the 0.10-per-minute slope lies between previously successful slopes at this starting composition.

Increase the endpoint one grid step to shorten retention relative to injection 18. This probes the steepest fully resolving slope near the successful compact method, with the middle pair expected to be the limiting separation.

Raise temperature one step to test whether the middle pair’s small resolution deficit can be recovered while shortening retention. Earlier temperature trends favor that pair but compress the first pair, so this tests the selectivity trade-off directly.

Lower both gradient endpoints by one grid step, preserving injection 20’s slope while increasing early retention. This tests whether the first pair can regain full resolution without losing the temperature-assisted middle-pair separation.

Return to the fastest fully resolved starting composition and temperature, increasing the slope only slightly from injection 16. This probes whether its small middle-pair resolution margin permits any further reduction in last-peak time.

Back off from 55 to 50 °C to restore early-pair resolution in injection 21’s compact gradient. The middle pair’s margin should accommodate this temperature change, yielding another maximum-score method with better early retention.

Back off injection 22’s endpoint by one grid step to recover full middle-pair resolution. This slightly shallower gradient should provide more resolution margin than the fastest maximum-score method, with only a modest increase in retention time.

Use the final injection to test a more conservative compact gradient near the fastest maximum-score method, lowering its endpoint one step to improve resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the observed last-peak elution fraction, so all six compounds should remain within the gradient.
